newsitem.title: USA: Oil surges but gains pared as market weighs Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Oil surges but gains pared as market weighs Iraq.

text.p: Oil prices in New York surged nearly five percent on Tuesday after the latest U.S./Iraqi confrontation but the gains were pared as traders and analysts took a circumscribed view of its likely impact.

U.S. benchmark West Texas crude futures for October delivery rose $2.00 to a four-month high of $24.25 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange after the U.S. bombed military targets in Iraq in retaliation for weekend attacks on internationally-protected Kurdish zones in the north of the country.

The United Nations Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali over the weekend suspended implementation of Iraq's oil-for-food accord which would have allowed exports of up to $2 billion of oil over six months to pay for food and medicines for ordinary Iraqis suffering under sanctions since Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Prior to Iraq's aggression exports looked set to resume sometime in September.
Also, a U.S. envoy to the U.N. and the State Department both indicated on Tuesday that it would be some time, perhaps several months, before the oil deal could be put back on track.
But the early gains eroded as oil traders weighed other factors likely to come into play.
"Oil prices were already up in the latter part of August partly because of fears of political risk in a nebulous sense," said Irene King, chief oil economist at J.P. Morgan.
"It started from a high price and what you got today was the other shoe dropping. It is no longer a high price built on fluff but there is a real reason," she added.
But the gains were held in check as the market looked ahead to the likely impact in the fourth quarter.
The amount of oil that Iraq was expected to export -- around 700,000 barrels a day -- "was not that big a deal," said Phillip Verleger, an analyst at Charles Rivers Associates in Washington.

"The (International Energy Agency, a Paris-based OECD energy thing tank) is telling us that 1.7 million barrels a day of incremental oil is coming at us in the fourth quarter, excluding Iraq," said Verleger.
"If that arrives, and I think it will, then prices will be depressed," he adds.

But the thin inventory levels which U.S. refiners have been running in anticipation of Iraqi and other extra oil, and as a way of saving on capital expenditure, has meant an exaggerrated reaction to any disruptions which have occurred in the past two years, analysts said.
"The fourth quarter is going to be tight in the absence of Iraqi oil but there is a limit to how high the price can go," J.P. Morgan's King said.

If high oil prices this winter lead to U.S. voter protests over heating oil costs in the way that soaring gasoline prices did last spring then the administration will need to act again, possibly through more oil sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to curb the market, King reckons.
"My best guess is that maybe it adds a buck (to oil prices in the fourth quarter)," said Vincent Farrell, an energy sector analyst at fund manager Spears, Benzak, Salomon and Farrel.
"I don't think it is that big a deal for the oil market or for energy stocks. It involves only 700,000 barrels a day which the market long-ago accommodated psychologically," Farrell said.
